extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biography of William Goldman covering his career as a novelist, playwright and screenwriter, with anecdotes and quotations that illustrate his craft, habits, and the qualities critics praised. Useful as a case study for screenwriting, adaptation, and storytelling practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling clarity and artful manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: IGN described Goldman's script for All the President's Men as "a model of storytelling clarity... and artful manipulation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tells that clarity of storytelling and skillful structuring/manipulation of material are evaluative hallmarks of strong screenwriting; All the President's Men is presented as an exemplar. Use clear narrative cause/effect and shape scenes to guide audience understanding and emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the lowest common denominator; upend expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sean Egan said Goldman's achievements were made "without ever lunging for the lowest common denominator... [he] has never let his populism overwhelm a glittering intelligence and penchant for upending expectation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favours writing that balances popular appeal with intelligence and surprise. Good work can be accessible yet subversive of clichéd outcomes—seek to surprise readers/viewers without sacrificing craft or clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid drafting / ability to produce quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman repeatedly wrote long works in very short timeframes (The Temple of Gold in less than three weeks; his second novel in a little more than a week; No Way to Treat a Lady in two weeks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that prolific, fast drafting can be a productive mode for some writers. Speed can help capture momentum and voice, though it may not be universal advice; the page uses these instances as evidence of Goldman's working method and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling emotional pain effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman: "I think I have a way with pain. When I come to that kind of sequence I have a certain confidence that I can make it play. Because I come from such a dark corner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional honesty and skillful rendering of painful sequences is a valued craft element; writers who can convincingly render suffering can make scenes 'play'—i.e., resonate with audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathetic characters facing tragic fates
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman observed, "Someone pointed out to me that the most sympathetic characters in my books always died miserably."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using tragic outcomes for sympathetic characters is a recurring artistic choice in Goldman's work—an evaluative pattern showing willingness to sacrifice comfort for emotional impact. It signals that compelling drama can come from subverting reader expectations about protagonists' fates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation and screenplay adaptation proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman adapted many works (e.g., The Princess Bride, Marathon Man, Magic, Misery) and won awards including an Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for All the President's Men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful adaptation requires translating source material into effective cinematic storytelling; Goldman's career and accolades are presented as evidence of high competence here. Examples and awards demonstrate adaptation as a distinct evaluative skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script doctoring and uncredited rewriting
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman served as an uncredited "script doctor" on numerous films (Twins, A Few Good Men, Indecent Proposal, Last Action Hero, Fierce Creatures, etc.), doing rewriting to improve others' scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to revise and strengthen existing screenplays—sometimes uncredited—is an important, professional craft skill. The page frames it as a common industry practice and a measure of a writer's practical usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing commercial viability and artistic goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman said: "Many movies that get made are not long on art and are long on commerce. This was a project that seemed it might be both. You don't get many and you can't turn them down."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights a practical evaluative tension: choose projects that can achieve both commercial success and artistic merit when possible. Screening project suitability involves assessing market realities alongside creative ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentoring and passing on craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman served as a mentor to a number of writers (e.g., Aaron Sorkin); other writers (Tony Gilroy, Scott Frank) noted his influence and mentorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentorship and advising are part of a professional writer's contribution; the page treats Goldman's mentoring as an aspect of his legacy and as a soft skill/criteria by which senior writers are valued in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crafting memorable lines / quotable dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldman wrote the famous line "Follow the money" in All the President's Men (a line often discussed and sometimes misattributed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorable, quotable lines can be a sign of strong screenwriting and help a script's cultural impact. The page uses this as an example of Goldman's ability to create enduring dialogue and phrases.
